Let us prove (i). If A is a direct limit lim→ Aᵢ, then

H⁰(𝓜ₙ, A ⊗ ωᵏ) = lim→ H⁰(𝓜ₙ, Aᵢ ⊗ ωᵏ).

It therefore suffices to treat the case in which A is a finitely generated ℤ[ζₙ]-module. If the f_{gφ} vanish, (2.4) shows that φ vanishes on the formal completion of 𝓜ₙ along infinity. The support of φ, disjoint from at least one point of every irreducible component of every geometric fibre of 𝓜ₙ, is therefore finite over ℤ[ζₙ]. Since 𝓜ₙ is Cohen–Macaulay over ℤ[ζₙ], and since A ⊗ ωᵏ is locally the inverse image of a module over ℤ[ζₙ], this is absurd if φ ≠ 0.

Let us prove (ii). Let Spec(D̂) be the sum of the formal completions of 𝓜ₙ along the sections at infinity gfₙ (g ∈ SL(2, ℤ/n)). The expansions at the cusps define a map

H⁰(𝓜ₙ, A ⊗ ωᵏ) → A ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} D̂.

We prove (ii) by considering the following diagram, whose second row is exact because D̂ is flat over ℤ[ζₙ]:

0 → H⁰(𝓜ₙ, B ⊗ ωᵏ) → H⁰(𝓜ₙ, A ⊗ ωᵏ) → H⁰(𝓜ₙ, A/B ⊗ ωᵏ)
↓                         ↓                         ↓
0 → B ⊗ D̂ → A ⊗ D̂ → A/B ⊗ D̂.

Theorem 3.10. (i) One has

H⁰(𝓜ₙ, ωᵏ) ⊗_{ℤ[ζₙ]} ℚ(ζₙ) ≃ H⁰(𝓜ₙ ⊗ ℚ, ωᵏ).

(ii) Let φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜ₙ ⊗ ℚ, ωᵏ), let fφ(q) = ∑ aᵢqⁱ (i ∈ (1/n)ℤ, aᵢ ∈ ℚ(ζₙ)) be the Fourier-series expansion of φ at fₙ, and let π be a place of ℚ(ζₙ). Then

νπ(fφ) = deg(fₙ) inf(νπ(aᵢ))

is the order of the zero (or the negative of the order of the pole) of φ at the generic point of the irreducible component of the fibre of 𝓜ₙ at π that meets the section at infinity fₙ.

From the point of view adopted here, this theorem is trivial; it follows from

Corollary 3.11. Let ∑ aᵢqⁱ be the Fourier-series expansion of φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜ₙ ⊗ ℚ, ωᵏ). The denominators of the aᵢ are bounded.

Corollary 3.12. Let π be a place of ℚ(ζₙ) of characteristic p, let pᵐ be the largest power of p dividing n, and let g be an element of SL(2, ℤ/n) whose image in SL(2, ℤ/pᵐ) lies in the upper-triangular group. Then

νπ(fφ) = νπ(f_{gφ}).

Indeed, the cusps fₙ and gfₙ meet the same irreducible component in characteristic p.

Corollary 3.13. If the expansion at one cusp of φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜ₙ ⊗ ℚ, ωᵏ) has coefficients in ℤ[ζₙ][1/n], then the expansions at the other cusps have the same property.

3.14. Let φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜ₙ, ωᵏ). If π is a place of ℚ(ζₙ) of characteristic p and the first coefficients of the Fourier-series expansion of φ are divisible by π, the reduction of φ modulo π vanishes to some order at the point at infinity fₙ. Write ν(π,g,φ) for the order of the zero of gφ:

if f_{gφ}(q) = ∑ aᵢqⁱ (i ∈ (1/n)ℤ), then aᵢ ≡ 0 (π) for ni < ν(π,g,φ).

The degree of ωᵏ on 𝓜ₙ can be calculated using φ. The result is already known (cf. VI 4.4). Carrying out the calculation gives:

Corollary 3.14. Let π be a place of ℚ(ζₙ) of characteristic p, let pᵐ be the largest power of p dividing n, and let φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜ₙ, ωᵏ). As g runs through the set BSL of elements of SL(2, ℤ/n) whose image in SL(2, ℤ/pᵐ) lies in the upper-triangular group, one has

|SL(2, ℤ/n)|⁻¹ ∑_{g∈BSL} ν(π,g,φ) ≤ |ℙ¹(ℤ/pᵐ)|⁻¹ k/12.

For n = 1, this result may be restated as follows.

Corollary 3.15. Let p be a prime number and let φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜₁, ωᵏ) be a modular form with series expansion fφ(q) = ∑ aₙqⁿ. Then

νp(fφ) = inf{νp(aᵢ) | i ≤ k/12}.

In other words, to verify that the coefficients of a modular form of weight k are divisible by a power of p, it suffices to verify this for those whose index is ≤ k/12.

3.16. One can also relate what happens on the various irreducible components in characteristic p. As an example, we shall treat the case of modular forms of level Γ₀(p). The same arguments apply to the study, at p, of modular forms of level Γ₀(p) ∩ Γ(n), with n prime to p. Passing to such a level would spare us the use of fractional intersection numbers, introduced on the model of VI 4.

3.17. Let φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜_{Γ₀(p)} ⊗ ℚ, ωᵏ). Such a form has two “expansions at the cusps.”

a) Evaluate φ on the Tate curve 𝔾̄ₘ^q/qℤ over ℤ[[q]] ⊗ ℚ, equipped with its subgroup μp (1.16.3); one obtains

₁fφ(q)·(dx/x)ᵏ, with ₁fφ(q) ∈ ℤ[[q]] ⊗ ℚ.

b) Evaluate φ on the Tate curve

𝔾̄ₘ^{q¹ᐟᵖ}/qℤ over ℤ[[q¹ᐟᵖ]] ⊗ ℚ,

equipped with its subgroup isomorphic to ℤ/p generated by q. One obtains

₂fφ(q)·(dx/x)ᵏ, with ₂fφ(q) ∈ ℤ[[q¹ᐟᵖ]] ⊗ ℚ.

For ℓ ≠ p, the ℓ-adic valuations of ₁fφ and ₂fφ (the lower bound of the ℓ-adic valuations of the coefficients) coincide. We shall write ν₁(φ) and ν₂(φ), or simply ν₁ and ν₂, for the p-adic valuations of ₁fφ and ₂fφ.

3.18. We extend the involution w (V.1.3) to modular forms as follows. To an elliptic curve C/S equipped with a subgroup A ⊂ C[p], the form wφ assigns the inverse image in ωᵏ of the section φ(C/A, C[p]/A) of (ω_{(C/A)/S})ᵏ. One has

wwφ = pᵏφ.

One checks that

₁f_{wφ}(q) = pᵏ ₂fφ(qᵖ),

₂f_{wφ}(q) = ₁fφ(q¹ᐟᵖ).

Consequently

(ν₁(wφ), ν₂(wφ)) = (k + ν₂(φ), ν₁(φ)),

and ν₂ − ν₁ + k/2 changes sign when one passes from φ to wφ.

3.19. We propose to estimate ν₁ − ν₂. This number does not change when φ is multiplied by an integer; we may therefore suppose that

φ ∈ H⁰(𝓜_{Γ₀(p)}, ωᵏ).

Assume that φ is not identically zero. If N₁ and N₂ are the two irreducible components of 𝓜_{Γ₀(p)} ⊗ 𝔽p, corresponding respectively to curves (C,A) with A infinitesimal and A discrete, the divisor of φ may be written

div(φ) = D + ν₁N₁ + ν₂N₂,

where the divisor D meets N₁ and N₂ at only finitely many points. On the regular stack 𝓜_{Γ₀(p)}, div(p) = N₁ + N₂, whence the vanishing of the intersection numbers

(N₁ + N₂, N₁) = (N₁ + N₂, N₂) = 0.

On N₁ ≃ 𝓜₁ ⊗ 𝔽p, ω has degree 1/24; therefore

(div(φ), N₁) = k/24.

Similarly, since on 𝓜_{Γ₀(p)} the degree of ω is (1/24)[𝓜_{Γ₀(p)}:𝓜₁] = (p+1)/24, one has

deg(D) = (D,N₁) + (D,N₂) = (p+1)k/24.

By VI.4.9, (N₂,N₁) = (p−1)/24.

One has

(D + ν₁N₁ + ν₂N₂, N₁) = (D,N₁) + ν₁(N₁+N₂,N₁) + (ν₂−ν₁)(N₂,N₁)

= ½((D,N₁)+(D,N₂)) + ½((D,N₁)−(D,N₂)) + (ν₂−ν₁+k/2)(N₂,N₁) − (k/2)(N₂,N₁).

Substituting the expressions above gives

½·k·(p+1)/24 + ½((D,N₁)−(D,N₂)) + (ν₂−ν₁+k/2)(p−1)/24 − (k/2)·(p−1)/24 = k/24.

Thus

(ν₂−ν₁+k/2)(p−1)/24 = ½((D,N₂)−(D,N₁)).

Proposition 3.20. One has

ν₂−ν₁+k/2 = ½·24/(p−1) ((D,N₂)−(D,N₁)),

(D,N₁) + (D,N₂) = k·(p+1)/24,

and hence

|ν₂−ν₁+k/2| ≤ ½·k·(p+1)/(p−1).

4. Comparison with transcendental theory.

4.1. We denote by D the open unit disc contained in ℂ, by q the usual coordinate on D (the inclusion D ↪ ℂ), and by D* the punctured disc D − {0}.

We denote by D[q¹ᐟᵏ] the Riemann surface of q¹ᐟᵏ: it is a copy of the unit disc, whose usual coordinate is called q¹ᐟᵏ, equipped with the map u : D[q¹ᐟᵏ] → D such that

q ∘ u = (q¹ᐟᵏ)ᵏ.

4.2. A construction identical to Construction 1.1 gives an analytic space 𝔾̄ₘ^q over D; translation by the section q (x₁ = 1) defines an action of ℤ on 𝔾̄ₘ^q, and this action is free (because |q| < 1). Passing to the quotient gives an analytic space 𝔾̄ₘ^q/qℤ over D, which is a family of generalized elliptic curves parametrized by D (the Tate curve).

The fibre of the morphism 𝔾̄ₘ^q/qℤ → D* at the point q ∈ D* is the elliptic curve ℂ*/qℤ ≃ ℂ/(ℤ + (log q)/(2πi)·ℤ).

4.3. Similarly, the k-gon Tate curve over D[q¹ᐟᵏ] is the quotient

𝔾̄ₘ^{q¹ᐟᵏ}/qℤ.

4.4. Constructions 4.2 and 1.15 are compatible in the following sense. There is a coherent system of isomorphisms of analytic spaces

(𝔾̄ₘ^q/qℤ, analytic, restricted to Spec(ℂ[[q]]/(qᴺ)) ⊂ D) ≃ ((𝔾̄ₘ^q/qℤ, algebraic) ⊗_{ℤ[[q]]} ℂ[[q]]/(qᴺ))^{an}.
